newsitem.title: TURKEY: NATO chief in talks on Turkey's place in Europe.
newsitem.headline: NATO chief in talks on Turkey's place in Europe.

text.p: NATO chief Javier Solana met Turkish officials on Thursday to discuss expansion of the alliance, Ankara's ties with rival member Greece and the broader issue of overwhelmingly Moslem Turkey's place in Europe.
"We are facing the moments of very important decisions, 1997 is going to be a crucial year," said Solana of NATO's planned July summit to consider expanding eastward.
He was speaking ahead of talks with Necmettin Erbakan, Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, who reiterated Ankara's view that NATO expansion and Turkey's relations with Europe were linked.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo on Tuesday said Europe faced difficulties in fully embracing Turkey, ranging from its human rights record to its religious identity.

Thurday's meeting was marred by news of an exchange of fire by Turkish and Greek Cypriots overnight in the buffer zone dividing the Mediterranean island after Greek Cypriots were said to have attempted to pull down a Turkish flag.

"At 0300 hours (0100 GMT) our patrol guards spotted two armed men attempting to lower our flag and three other armed men were spotted taking up position," Turkish Cypriot official Taner Etkin told Reuters in Nicosia.
U.N. sources confirmed shooting had taken place but the Greek Cypriot government spokesman categorically denied the army was involved in any incident.
Solana's trip comes at a time of renewed tension over Cyprus, which plans to buy Russian missiles to counter Turkish aircraft. Turkey has threatened a military strike if they are installed.
NATO officials fear conflict between members Greece and Turkey on its southern flank could harm plans to reform the alliance and take in new members from former communist east Europe.
Solana, who visited both countries last year, will urge Ankara to accept confidence-building measures. He is expected to visit Athens toward the end of the month.
He stressed Ankara's importance within the NATO alliance ahead of meetings with Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller and leading military officials.
"I would publicly say that Turkey is playing a very, very important role in NATO as it has in the past," Solana told reporters after meeting Defence Minister Turhan Tayan.

Ciller has warned that Ankara could veto NATO's eastward expansion if Turkey's aspirations for closer ties with the EU remain frustrated. Turkey could also block plans to lend NATO equipment to the Western European Union (WEU), in which Ankara only has observer status.
Solana said ahead of his visit that he did not think Turkey would block anything, but Erbakan stressed Ciller's warning was an expression of Ankara's view.
After van Mierlo's comments Turkey sought reassurance on Wednesday that its Moslem identity would not block entry into the EU.

"We were openly told the EU is not a Christian club. We want to believe that these statements of the EU's high-ranking officials were sincere," Turkish Foreign Ministry spokesman Omer Akbel told a news conference.
Ninety-nine percent Moslem but secular Turkey signed an association agreement with what is now the European Union as long ago as 1963 and formally applied to join the bloc in 1987.
